issues.item: Threat: missing/none selected despite multiple current-danger and exposure-related items
issues.explanation: The profile contains several items implying an active sense of present threat or exposure (e.g., 'World is Dangerous', 'Exposed to Others', concealment to avoid being noticed), yet the Threat component is entirely absent. For this trauma type, such items would usually cohere with at least some explicit threat content; the omission makes the cross-node picture clinically uneven.

'World is Dangerous' expresses a broad ongoing threat belief, but the formulation specifies no active links into or out of Threat and no Threat items are endorsed. This makes the appraisal sit awkwardly in the formulation because it functions more like a threat belief than an isolated negative self-appraisal.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Concealing Clothing: wear concealing clothing to avoid being noticed
issues.explanation: 'Concealing Clothing ... to avoid being noticed' implies active management of current interpersonal threat/visibility. With Threat completely unrepresented and no Trigger→Threat or Maladaptive Strategies→Threat linkage in the formulation, this strategy lacks a clear matching symptom target in the rest of the profile.

Threat: missing/none selected despite multiple current-danger and exposure-related items

issues.item: Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
issues.explanation: The Threat node is not clinically coherent here. 'Flashbacks' and 'Physical Reactivity' are re-experiencing/arousal responses rather than threat appraisals, while the only genuine threat appraisal selected is 'Threat from Strangers.' That mixes different constructs within one node.

vignette:
Darnell was 25 when he first came to treatment, a single North American man working as a housekeeper in a hotel, where his days were structured around other people’s messes, their private routines, and the need to stay unobtrusive. He had grown up with a caregiver who was physically abusive, and the details of that childhood still felt close enough to him that he could be pulled back into them by the wrong sound, the wrong darkness, or even the wrong texture under his fingertips. The specific texture that now set him on edge was one that reminded him of the place and circumstances of the abuse, and he could not touch it without a sudden tightening in his chest and a wish to get away from whatever he was doing. In the years after the abuse, he had learned to move through the world as if danger could appear at any time, and as a child he had often felt that there was no reliable way to know who would hurt him and when.

What disturbed him most as an adult was how the old memories still returned. When they came, they did not feel distant or narrated from a safe place. They arrived with such force that he had to stop whatever he was doing because the emotion became overwhelming. He described the memory as if it were a film that played over and over, always with the same frightening scenes and same unbearable sense of being back there. At times, the return was even more vivid: he felt the abuse across all his senses at once, as though the past had stepped into the present without warning. In those moments he could smell, hear, and feel enough to lose his bearings, and for a few seconds he was not thinking about remembering at all; he was simply there, swallowed by it.

Nighttime had remained especially hard. If he woke in the dark, or if he found himself moving through a room with no lights, his body reacted before he had time to orient himself. The dark made him feel exposed and unprepared, as if he were once again a child waiting for something bad to happen. At work, this showed up in small but important ways. When his housekeeping shifts required him to enter dim guest corridors or clean rooms before full daylight, he became more watchful and tense, scanning the spaces and feeling a need to get through them quickly. He did not like being alone with another person in those settings, either. He would arrange his tasks so that he was not isolated with coworkers, supervisors, or anyone else if he could help it, and if circumstances made that unavoidable, he felt himself bracing as though something could turn dangerous without warning.

He also found himself pulling away from responsibility in order to feel safer. Over time, he began giving up important tasks when he anticipated that they might expose him to reminders of the abuse. This had practical consequences at work and in his daily life, where he became known as someone who needed to step back, take longer breaks, or avoid certain assignments. He did not experience this as laziness or indifference. In his mind, it was a way of staying out of reach. Alongside that, he often drifted off into a world of his own, mentally leaving situations that felt too close to the old fear. It was not a dramatic escape, more a quiet slipping away, but it let him get through moments that otherwise felt intolerable.

Darnell also carried the belief that other people could see what had happened to him just by looking at him. He felt marked in some way, as though the past sat on his face and in his posture, visible to strangers who would understand that he was not whole in the way they were. Along with that came a painful sense of being less than fully human, more like an object than a person. He did not speak about these beliefs casually; they seemed to shape how he moved through public spaces, how guarded he became, and how difficult it was for him to trust that anyone would treat him gently. This was part of why he was so careful never to be alone with another person if he could avoid it, and why he remained on edge even in ordinary interactions.

More recently, the sound of children crying had become another sharp trigger. Hearing it in a hallway, on the street, or in the hotel could bring him right back to the helplessness of childhood, not because he wanted to think about the past, but because his body and mind seemed to recognize the sound as something tied to those early years. He would tense, go still, and feel a rush of physical alarm. What finally brought him to seek help was that these reactions were becoming harder to keep hidden, especially at work, where he could no longer easily pass them off as being tired or distracted. He came in wanting relief from the intensity of the memories and the constant sense of watchfulness, but he was also afraid that what had happened to him had permanently changed the way others would see him. More than anything, he hoped to stop feeling like danger was always just around the corner, and to learn whether there was a way to be alone in a room, in the dark, or with his own mind without bracing for the past to return.
